meta.title: Polyglot Core — a beginner course across 7 languages
meta.license: Translations & IPA are facts cross-checked against Wiktionary (CC-BY-SA, attributed via Kaikki — IPA pulled from the live photon dictionary at polingual.agfarms.dev); example sentences are original and beginner-simple.

atoms.note: Romance '1' all descend from Latin 'unus'; English 'one' and German 'eins' are the Germanic branch of the same Indo-European root *óynos.
Every form here comes from Indo-European *dwóh₁: Latin 'duo' → Romance, while English 'two' and German 'zwei' kept the Germanic shape (the 'd→t/z' shift is Grimm's Law).
Latin 'tres' gives Spanish/Portuguese 'tres/três' directly; the English 'th' and German 'dr' both trace to the same *tréyes — once you see 'tri-' you see them all.
Romance 'qu-' forms (cuatro, quatre, quattro, quatro) all come from Latin 'quattuor'; English 'four' and German 'vier' kept the 'f/v' Germanic reflex of the same *kʷetwóres.
Latin 'quinque' → 'cinco/cinq/cinque'; English 'five' and German 'fünf' show the Germanic 'f' for the same root *pénkʷe (think 'penta-' in Greek loanwords).
Almost transparent: Latin 'sex' → 'seis/six/sei/seis', and English 'six' / German 'sechs' barely diverge. The shared 's-' root *swéḱs makes this one of the easiest cognates.
Latin 'septem' (cf. 'September', the old 7th month) → 'siete/sept/sette/sete'; English 'seven' and German 'sieben' descend from the same *septḿ̥.
Latin 'octo' (cf. 'octopus', 'October') → 'ocho/huit/otto/oito'; English 'eight' and German 'acht' come from the same *oḱtṓ — the 'ct' often softens to a vowel in Romance.
Latin 'novem' (cf. 'November', old 9th month) → 'nueve/neuf/nove'; English 'nine' and German 'neun' share the same *h₁néwn̥. All start with 'n-'.
Latin 'decem' (cf. 'decimal', 'December') → 'diez/dix/dieci/dez'; English 'ten' and German 'zehn' descend from the same *déḱm̥. The 'dec-' prefix you know from math is right here.
Latin 'ego' (the source of the English psychology term) gives Italian 'io' and Portuguese 'eu'; English 'I' and German 'ich' descend from a separate but related *éǵ-.

The informal 'you' is one of the most stable words in Europe: Latin 'tu' is unchanged in Spanish/French/Italian/Portuguese, and German 'du' is the same *túh₂. English alone replaced 'thou' with the old plural 'you'.
Romance 'he' (él, il, ele) descends from Latin 'ille' (that one); Italian 'lui' is from the same demonstrative. English 'he' and German 'er' are a separate Germanic set.
The feminine 'she' in Romance (ella, elle, ela) is the feminine of Latin 'ille' → 'illa'. Note the '-a/-e' feminine ending lighting up across Spanish, French, and Portuguese.
Latin 'nos' is right there in French 'nous', Italian 'noi', Portuguese 'nós', and the 'nos-' of Spanish 'nosotros'. English 'we' and German 'wir' are the Germanic *wéi instead.
Romance plural 'they' (ellos, ils, eles) is the plural of Latin 'ille'; Italian 'loro' is from Latin 'illorum' (of those). English 'they' is unusually a Norse loan, not native Germanic.

Latin 'esse' is the parent of Spanish/Portuguese 'ser', French 'être', and Italian 'essere'. The root *h₁es- also surfaces in English 'is' and German 'ist'. (Spanish/Portuguese split a second 'to be' — estar — for states.)

example.en: It is good to be here.

atoms.note: Romance 'to have' (haber, avoir, avere, haver) all come from Latin 'habere'. English 'have' and German 'haben' look identical but are a coincidental Germanic root *habjaną — same meaning, different family.
Italian and Spanish 'sì/sí' come from Latin 'sic' (thus, so); Portuguese 'sim' is from 'sic' too. French 'oui' is from 'hoc ille' (this one). German 'ja' and English 'yes' are Germanic.
Latin 'non' is the root of every 'no' here: Spanish/Italian 'no', French 'non', Portuguese 'não'. The 'n-' negation runs all the way to English 'no' and German 'nein' via *ne.
French 'bonjour' is literally 'good day'. Latin 'salve' (be well) survives in the English 'salutation'. Italian 'ciao' actually comes from Venetian 'schiavo' (your servant).
Spanish 'gracias' and Italian 'grazie' come from Latin 'gratias' (thanks, favors) — the same root as English 'grace' and 'gratitude'. French 'merci' is from Latin 'merces' (reward).

Spanish/Portuguese 'por favor' and Italian 'per favore' literally mean 'by/for favor' (Latin 'favor'). French 's'il vous plaît' means 'if it pleases you' — sharing the root of English 'please' (Latin 'placere').
Spanish 'adiós' and Portuguese 'adeus' literally mean 'to God' (a Dios), as does French 'adieu'. Latin 'vale' (be strong / farewell) is the classical goodbye — the root of 'valid' and 'value'.
Spanish/Portuguese 'este' and Italian 'questo' (from Latin 'eccum istum') point to the near demonstrative. English 'this' and German 'dieser' share the Germanic 'th/d' demonstrative root.
The far demonstrative: Spanish 'ese', Portuguese 'esse', Italian 'quello' from Latin 'ille' / 'eccum illum' — the same 'ille' that became the Romance words for 'he' and 'the'.
Spanish/Portuguese 'aquí/aqui' and Italian 'qui' trace to Latin 'hic' (here). English 'here' and German 'hier' are a separate Germanic 'h-' word — but the meanings line up cleanly.
Romance 'there' (allí, là, lì, ali) carry the 'l-' of Latin 'illic' / 'illac' — the demonstrative 'ille' again. English 'there' and German 'dort' are the Germanic counterpart.
All Romance forms descend from Latin 'aqua' (think 'aquarium', 'aquatic'); English 'water' is Germanic (cf. German 'Wasser'), from the parallel root *wódr̥.
Romance 'bread' (pan, pain, pane, pão) all come from Latin 'panis' — the root of 'pantry', 'companion' (one you share bread with), and 'empanada'. English 'bread' and German 'Brot' are Germanic.

Spanish, Italian, and Portuguese keep Latin 'casa' (cottage) unchanged. French chose 'maison' (from Latin 'mansio', a dwelling — root of 'mansion'). English 'house' and German 'Haus' are Germanic twins.
Romance 'friend' (amigo, ami, amico) is from Latin 'amicus', built on 'amare' (to love) — the same root as 'amiable' and 'amity'. English 'friend' and German 'Freund' are Germanic.

Spanish/Portuguese 'día/dia' come straight from Latin 'dies'. French 'jour' and Italian 'giorno' took a different Latin path through 'diurnum' (daily) — the root of 'journal' and 'journey'. English 'day' / German 'Tag' are Germanic.

A beautiful cognate set: Latin 'nox' (stem 'noct-', as in 'nocturnal') gives noche/nuit/notte/noite, and the same root *nókʷts gives English 'night' and German 'Nacht'. Every form keeps the 'n-' and a 't/ch'.

Latin 'sol' (root of 'solar') is nearly untouched in Spanish/Portuguese 'sol' and Italian 'sole'; French 'soleil' adds a diminutive. English 'sun' and German 'Sonne' are the Germanic side of the same *sóh₂wl̥.
Romance 'moon' (luna, lune, luna, lua) all come from Latin 'luna' (root of 'lunar', 'lunatic'). English 'moon' and German 'Mond' descend from a different root *mḗh₁n̥s — also the source of 'month'.

example.es: La luna está llena esta noche.

atoms.note: Romance 'book' (libro, livre, libro, livro) all come from Latin 'liber' — root of 'library' and 'libretto'. English 'book' and German 'Buch' come from the Germanic word for beech wood, on which early runes were carved.

French 'chien', Italian 'cane', and Portuguese 'cão' come from Latin 'canis' (root of 'canine'). Spanish broke ranks with 'perro' (uncertain origin). English 'dog' and German 'Hund' (cf. 'hound') are Germanic.

Romance 'hand' (mano, main, mano, mão) all come from Latin 'manus' — the root of 'manual', 'manage', 'manuscript'. Note 'mano' is feminine even though it ends in '-o'. English/German 'hand' is the Germanic word.
Romance 'eye' (ojo, œil, occhio, olho) all come from Latin 'oculus' — root of 'ocular', 'binoculars', 'inoculate'. English 'eye' and German 'Auge' descend from the parallel root *h₃ókʷs.

One of the oldest cognates in the family: Latin 'mater' (root of 'maternal', 'matrix') gives madre/mère/madre/mãe, and the same *méh₂tēr gives English 'mother' and German 'Mutter'. Every form starts with 'm-'.
Latin 'pater' (root of 'paternal', 'patriarch') gives padre/père/padre/pai. English 'father' and German 'Vater' come from the same *ph₂tḗr — the Latin 'p' became Germanic 'f' by Grimm's Law.

Spanish/Portuguese 'comer' is from Latin 'comedere' (to eat up). French 'manger' and Italian 'mangiare' come from Latin 'manducare' (to chew). English 'eat' and German 'essen' descend from Latin's cousin root 'edere' (*h₁ed-).
Romance 'to drink' (beber, boire, bere, beber) all come from Latin 'bibere' — the root of 'imbibe' and 'beverage'. English 'drink' and German 'trinken' are a separate Germanic pair.

example.fr: Je bois de l'eau chaque jour.

atoms.note: Spanish/Portuguese 'ir' come directly from Latin 'ire' (to go) — the root of 'exit' (he/she goes out). French 'aller' and Italian 'andare' have separate Latin sources. English 'go' and German 'gehen' are Germanic.
Romance 'to come' (venir, venir, venire, vir) all come from Latin 'venire' — the root of 'adventure', 'convene', 'event'. English 'come' and German 'kommen' descend from the cousin root *gʷem-.
Romance 'to see' (ver, voir, vedere, ver) all come from Latin 'videre' — the root of 'video', 'vision', 'evident'. English 'see' and German 'sehen' are the Germanic pair.

French 'vouloir' and Italian 'volere' come from Latin 'velle' (to wish) — and so do English 'will' and German 'wollen', via the shared root *welh₁-. Spanish/Portuguese 'querer' took a different Latin verb, 'quaerere' (to seek).

Romance 'to know' (saber, savoir, sapere, saber) come from Latin 'sapere' (to be wise / taste) — root of 'savvy' and 'Homo sapiens'. Latin also had 'scire' (root of 'science'). English 'know' and German 'wissen' are Germanic.

Spanish 'hablar' and Portuguese 'falar' come from Latin 'fabulari' (to chat — root of 'fable'). French 'parler' and Italian 'parlare' come from 'parabolare' (root of 'parable', 'parley'). English 'speak'/German 'sprechen' are Germanic.

Romance 'to do/make' (hacer, faire, fare, fazer) all come from Latin 'facere' — the root of 'fact', 'factory', 'manufacture'. Spanish 'h-' is a silent leftover of Latin 'f-'. English 'do' and German 'machen' are Germanic.

Spanish/Portuguese/Italian 'dar/dare' come straight from Latin 'dare' (to give) — root of 'donate', 'data' (things given). French 'donner' is from the related 'donare'. English 'give'/German 'geben' are Germanic.
Romance 'good' (bueno, bon, buono, bom) all come from Latin 'bonus' — the root of 'bonus', 'bonafide', 'benefit'. English 'good' and German 'gut' are an unrelated Germanic pair.

Romance 'big' (grande, grand, grande, grande) all come from Latin 'grandis' — root of 'grand', 'grandeur'. Latin's other word, 'magnus' (root of 'magnify', 'magnitude'), survives in scientific vocabulary. English 'big' / German 'groß' are Germanic.

The Romance words for 'small' are a scattered family (pequeño, petit, piccolo, pequeno) tied to an expressive 'pikk-/pitt-' root for 'little'. Latin used 'parvus'. English 'small' and German 'klein' are Germanic.
A clean cognate: Latin 'novus' (root of 'novel', 'innovate', 'renovate') gives nuevo/nouveau/nuovo/novo, and the same *néwos gives English 'new' and German 'neu'. Every form keeps 'n-' + a 'v/w'.
Romance 'old' (viejo, vieux, vecchio, velho) come from Latin 'vetulus' (little-old), a diminutive of 'vetus' — the root of 'veteran' and 'inveterate'. English 'old' and German 'alt' are Germanic.

Romance 'hot' (caliente, chaud, caldo, quente) all come from Latin 'calidus' — the root of 'calorie', 'cauldron', 'nonchalant'. The 'cal-/chal-' is the heat. English 'hot' and German 'heiß' are Germanic.

Romance 'cold' (frío, froid, freddo, frio) all come from Latin 'frigidus' — the root of 'frigid', 'refrigerator'. English 'cold' and German 'kalt' are Germanic — and interestingly share a root with Latin 'gelidus' (gel/cold).

Spanish 'rojo', French 'rouge', Italian 'rosso' come from Latin 'russus/ruber' — root of 'ruby', 'rubric'. The whole family, including English 'red' and German 'rot', traces to *h₁rewdʰ-. Portuguese went its own way with 'vermelho' (from 'vermiculus', the red dye-worm).

Two families here: Spanish/Portuguese 'azul' is from Arabic 'lāzaward' (lapis lazuli), while French 'bleu', Italian 'blu', English 'blue', German 'blau' all share the Germanic root *blēwaz. Latin had no single common word; 'caeruleus' (sky-blue) is the classical term.
Romance 'green' (verde, vert, verde, verde) all come from Latin 'viridis' — root of 'verdant', 'verdure'. English 'green' and German 'grün' share a Germanic root with 'grow' and 'grass'.

Spanish 'negro', French 'noir', Italian 'nero' all come from Latin 'niger' — root of 'denigrate'. Portuguese commonly uses 'preto' (from Latin 'apprehensus', pressed-tight/dense). English 'black' and German 'schwarz' are Germanic.

Romance 'white' (blanco, blanc, bianco, branco) is borrowed from Germanic *blankaz (shining) — the same root as English 'blank'. Classical Latin used 'albus' (root of 'album', 'albino'). English 'white' / German 'weiß' are native Germanic.
Romance 'year' (año, an, anno, ano) all come from Latin 'annus' — root of 'annual', 'anniversary'. Spanish 'ñ' is a squeezed double-n. English 'year' and German 'Jahr' are Germanic.
A near-universal cognate: Latin 'nomen' (root of 'nominate', 'noun', 'nominal') gives nombre/nom/nome/nome, and the same *h₁nómn̥ gives English 'name' and German 'Name'. They all keep 'n-...-m'.

Spanish 'ciudad', Italian 'città', Portuguese 'cidade', and English 'city' all come from Latin 'civitas' (citizenry — root of 'civic', 'civilization'). French 'ville' is from 'villa' (farmstead). German 'Stadt' is Germanic.

example.en: I live in a big city.

atoms.note: Romance 'fire' (fuego, feu, fuoco, fogo) come from Latin 'focus' (hearth — yes, the same word as English 'focus'). Latin's poetic word was 'ignis' (root of 'ignite'). English 'fire' and German 'Feuer' descend from a separate root *péh₂wr̥.
Romance 'earth' (tierra, terre, terra, terra) all come from Latin 'terra' — root of 'territory', 'terrain', 'terrestrial'. English 'earth' and German 'Erde' are the Germanic pair.

example.it: La terra è la nostra casa.

atoms.note: Romance 'milk' (leche, lait, latte, leite) all come from Latin 'lac' (stem 'lact-') — root of 'lactose', 'lactic', 'latte'. English 'milk' and German 'Milch' are Germanic, though distantly related via *gʷálakts.

example.en: I drink milk in the morning.

atoms.note: Romance 'fish' (pez, poisson, pesce, peixe) all come from Latin 'piscis' — root of 'Pisces', 'piscine'. English 'fish' and German 'Fisch' are the Germanic reflex of the same root (Latin 'p' → Germanic 'f').

example.en: The fish is in the water.
example.es: El pez está en el agua.

atoms.note: A perfect cognate: Latin 'vinum' (root of 'vine', 'vintage', 'vinegar') gives vino/vin/vino/vinho, and the borrowed-into-Germanic 'Wein' and 'wine' too. Every form keeps the 'v/w' + 'n'.

Spanish 'palabra', Italian 'parola', Portuguese 'palavra' come from Latin 'parabola' (comparison — also the root of 'parable' and, via French, 'parole'). Latin 'verbum' (root of 'verb', 'verbal') links to English 'word' and German 'Wort'.

Spanish 'cabeza' and Portuguese 'cabeça' come from Latin 'capitia', from 'caput' (root of 'capital', 'captain', 'decapitate'). French 'tête' and Italian 'testa' come from Latin 'testa' (a pot — slang for the head). English 'head' and German 'Kopf' (originally 'cup') are Germanic.

Romance 'heart' (corazón, cœur, cuore, coração) all come from Latin 'cor' (stem 'cord-') — root of 'cordial', 'courage', 'record'. English 'heart' and German 'Herz' descend from the same *ḱḗr — once you spot the 'c/h' + 'r' you see them all.

Romance 'foot' (pie, pied, piede, pé) all come from Latin 'pes' (stem 'ped-') — root of 'pedal', 'pedestrian', 'pedestal'. English 'foot' and German 'Fuß' descend from the same *pṓds, with Latin 'p' → Germanic 'f'.
Romance 'tree' (árbol, arbre, albero, árvore) all come from Latin 'arbor' — root of 'arbor', 'arboretum'. English 'tree' and German 'Baum' are Germanic (Baum is the source of English 'beam').

Romance 'flower' (flor, fleur, fiore, flor) and English 'flower' all come from Latin 'flos' (stem 'flor-') — root of 'floral', 'flora', 'flourish'. German 'Blume' is Germanic (cf. English 'bloom' and 'blossom').

Almost every European 'cat' (gato, chat, gatto, gato, Katze, cat) descends from Late Latin 'cattus'. This word spread across the whole continent with the domestic cat itself — one of the most uniform cognates in the deck.

Romance 'horse' (caballo, cheval, cavallo, cavalo) come from Latin 'caballus' (workhorse, nag) — root of 'cavalry', 'chivalry', 'cavalier'. Classical Latin 'equus' (root of 'equestrian') lost out. English 'horse' and German 'Pferd' are Germanic.

Spanish 'pájaro' and Portuguese 'pássaro' come from Latin 'passer' (sparrow). Italian 'uccello' and French 'oiseau' come from Latin 'avicellus', a diminutive of 'avis' (root of 'aviary', 'aviation'). English 'bird' and German 'Vogel' are Germanic.

Spanish 'mujer' and Portuguese 'mulher' come from Latin 'mulier'. French 'femme' comes from Latin 'femina' (root of 'feminine'). Italian 'donna' is from 'domina' (lady — root of 'Madonna', 'dame'). English 'woman' and German 'Frau' are Germanic.

Romance 'man' (hombre, homme, uomo, homem) all come from Latin 'homo' (human being) — root of 'human', 'homage', 'Homo sapiens'. The silent Spanish/Portuguese 'h-' is the old Latin 'h'. English 'man' and German 'Mann' are Germanic.

French 'enfant' and English 'infant' both come from Latin 'infans' (literally 'not speaking'). Portuguese 'criança' is from Latin 'creare' (to create — cf. 'creature'). Spanish 'niño' and Italian 'bambino' are nursery words. German 'Kind' (cf. 'kin', 'kindergarten') is Germanic.

Romance 'to live' (vivir, vivre, vivere, viver) all come from Latin 'vivere' — root of 'vivid', 'survive', 'revive', 'vivacious'. English 'live' and German 'leben' descend from a separate Germanic root *libjaną.

Romance 'to read' (leer, lire, leggere, ler) all come from Latin 'legere' (to gather, choose, read) — root of 'legible', 'lecture', 'lesson', 'collect'. German 'lesen' shares the 'gather' sense too. English 'read' is the Germanic odd one out.

example.en: I read a book at night.
example.es: Leo un libro por la noche.

atoms.note: Romance 'to write' (escribir, écrire, scrivere, escrever) all come from Latin 'scribere' — root of 'scribe', 'describe', 'manuscript', 'script'. German 'schreiben' is borrowed from the same Latin verb. English 'write' is the Germanic odd one out.

Romance 'to love' (amar, aimer, amare, amar) all come from Latin 'amare' — root of 'amateur', 'amorous'. This is the verb behind the 'love' noun and 'I love you' entries in this deck. English 'love' and German 'lieben' are Germanic.

Spanish 'amarillo' and Portuguese 'amarelo' come from Latin 'amarellus' (bitterish). French 'jaune' and Italian 'giallo' come from Latin 'galbinus' (greenish-yellow). English 'yellow' and German 'gelb' share a Germanic root with 'gold' and 'glow'.

French 'beau', Italian 'bello', Portuguese 'belo' all come from Latin 'bellus' (pretty) — root of 'embellish' and the name 'Bella'. English 'beautiful' is from Latin 'bellus' too, via French 'beauté'. Classical Latin's main word was 'pulcher'. German 'schön' is Germanic.

'Zero' (cero, zéro, zero, zero) is a young word: from Italian 'zero', from Arabic 'sifr' (empty) — which also gives English 'cipher'. German 'null' and the Latin idea 'nihil' (nothing — root of 'annihilate', 'nihilism') express the same emptiness differently.

Romance 'today' (hoy, oggi, hoje, and the '-hui' inside French 'aujourd'hui') all come from Latin 'hodie' — itself a contraction of 'hoc die' (on this day). The 'day' word from this deck is hiding inside it. English 'today' and German 'heute' are Germanic.

Another build-your-own phrase: 'good' (bueno/bon/buono/bom) + 'night' (noche/nuit/notte/noite) — both already in this deck. Italian fuses them as 'buonanotte'. Once you know the parts, the greeting assembles itself.

The Romance 'cómo/come/como' all come from Latin 'quomodo' (in what way). Spanish/Portuguese/Italian use the verb 'estar/stare' (Latin 'stare', to stand) for state — the same root as English 'state' and 'stand'. German asks literally 'how goes it to you?'.

The Romance languages ask literally 'how do you call yourself?' — llamas/t'appelles/ti chiami/te chamas all use a reflexive verb from Latin 'clamare' (to call out) or 'appellare'. Latin instead asks 'what name is to you?', using the noun 'nomen' from this deck.

Spanish 'entiendo' and Portuguese 'entendo' come from Latin 'intendere' (to stretch toward, attend). French 'comprends' and Italian 'capisco' come from 'comprehendere' / 'capere' (to grasp) — the same image as English 'grasp the meaning'. Note the negators no/ne...pas/non from earlier in the deck.

Spanish 'dónde', Italian 'dove', Portuguese 'onde' all come from Latin 'unde' (from where) reinforced by 'de'. French 'où' is from Latin 'ubi'. The verb is 'estar/stare' again. German 'wo' and English 'where' share a Germanic question-word root.

French 'aime', Italian 'amo', Portuguese 'amo', and Latin 'amo' all come from Latin 'amare' (to love) — the root of 'amateur' (one who does it for love) and 'amorous'. Spanish often uses 'querer' (to want) for people. German 'lieben' connects to English 'love'.

Romance 'love' (amor, amour, amore, amor) all come from Latin 'amor' — root of 'amorous', 'enamored', 'paramour'. English 'love' and German 'Liebe' are Germanic, from *lewbʰ- (the same root that gives Latin 'libido').

Romance 'time' (tiempo, temps, tempo, tempo) all come from Latin 'tempus' — root of 'temporary', 'tempo', 'contemporary'. (In Spanish/Italian/Portuguese it also means 'weather'.) English 'time' and German 'Zeit' are Germanic.

Romance 'light' (luz, lumière, luce, luz) all come from Latin 'lux' (stem 'luc-') — root of 'lucid', 'translucent', 'Lucifer' (light-bearer). The same root *lewk- also gives English 'light' and German 'Licht'. A canon-tier word: light ties to the physics branch.

Spanish/Italian/Portuguese 'mente' come from Latin 'mens' (stem 'ment-') — root of 'mental', 'mention', 'comment'. English 'mind' is from the same *men- (to think). French 'esprit' (from 'spiritus') and German 'Geist' pick the 'spirit' sense instead. A canon-tier word tying to the mind branch.

example.en: A clear mind sees the truth.
example.es: Una mente clara ve la verdad.
example.it: Una mente chiara vede la verità.

atoms.note: Romance 'truth' (verdad, vérité, verità, verdade) all come from Latin 'veritas' — root of 'verify', 'verdict', 'very'. The '-dad/-té/-tà/-dade' endings all reflect Latin '-tas'. English 'truth' and German 'Wahrheit' are Germanic. A canon-tier word: truth underlies every branch.

Romance 'number' (número, nombre, numero, número) and English 'number' all come from Latin 'numerus' — root of 'numeral', 'enumerate', 'numerous'. German 'Zahl' is Germanic (cf. 'tale', a count). A canon-tier word tying to the mathematics branch.

example.it: Il sette è il mio numero.

atoms.note: Romance 'star' (estrella, étoile, stella, estrela) all come from Latin 'stella' — root of 'stellar', 'constellation'. English 'star' and German 'Stern' descend from the same *h₂stḗr. A canon-tier word tying to the cosmology branch.

This phrase recombines two words you already know: 'good' (bueno/bon/buono/bom) + 'day' (día/jour/giorno/dia). French and Italian fuse them into one word ('bonjour', 'buongiorno'). German says 'good morning' literally. Notice the building-block reuse.

A full sentence built from this deck: 'I' + 'to have' + 'one/a' + 'friend'. Note that Spanish 'tener' and Italian/French/Latin 'avere/avoir/habere' both render English 'have' — Spanish picked the 'hold' verb where the others kept Latin 'habere'.

example.en: The hill is fifty metres high.
example.it: La collina è alta cinquanta metri.
example.de: Der Hügel ist fünfzig Meter hoch.

example.en: The city has a thousand streets.

example.es: El viernes es mi día favorito.
example.it: Venerdì è il mio giorno preferito.

example.fr: La route est longue, le chemin long.
example.it: La strada è lunga, il cammino lungo.

example.es: La película es corta, el día corto.
Es una buena idea, un libro bueno.
example.de: Das ist ein gutes Buch, sehr gut.

example.en: The book is on the table.
example.es: El libro está en la mesa.
example.fr: Le livre est sur la table.
example.de: Das Buch ist auf dem Tisch.

example.en: The shop is on the right.
example.es: La tienda está a la derecha.
Ellos son pobres, un hombre pobre.

example.it: La stanza è pulita, il piatto pulito.

example.es: La caja está vacía, el vaso vacío.
example.it: La scatola è vuota, il vaso vuoto.

example.en: What do you want to say?
The cat is in the house.
example.fr: Le chat est dans la maison.
example.de: Die Katze ist in dem Haus.

example.en: The book is on the table.
example.es: El libro está sobre la mesa.
